segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. So sometimes, you break up with somebody, and you still talk. You're friendly. Some exes, you never speak with again. It's harsh, but everybody understands it when somebody's feelings are crushed. It's not unusual.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What is unusual is somebody who wants to be in touch with all their exes-- I mean, all of them, even the ones who never want to see his face again, the ones who feel really hurt and disappointed. Evan Roberts is a person who wants to reach out like that and become friends with the most hostile of his exes. It's a weird mission that one of our producers, Tobin Low, was curious about.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Evan made a list of 17 exes. By the time he and I met, he had talked with 16 of them over the last several years. It was nice to catch up, get their side of the story. But the more the thing had gone on, the more he realized this whole mission was actually just about ex number 17, someone he referred to as The Big Ex, a guy named Keith who, even when Evan reached out, did not want to talk. They'd broken up around New Year's. It was 2010. A couple of weeks after--

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I was on my bike, and I was going through the little atrium of the apartment building and getting the mail. And I got this card from Keith. And Keith repurposes cards and envelopes and puts stickers on them and stuff. So I opened it up at the mail-- like, I'm blocking the door. I'm sure I opened it up at the mailbox. And on the cover is a winter scene. And there's some blue dotted stickers he has on it. And where the sentiment of the card should have been was just a ripped-out hole.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith had torn out the part where there should have been "Merry Christmas" or "Happy holidays."

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: It was a void. And I saw through the hole onto my shoe on the floor.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: On the opposite flap, Keith wrote a note about how he thought he and Evan should stay away from each other. I think most people receiving a holiday card with the heartfelt sentiment surgically removed would think, message received. I will also cut you out of my life, ex-lover. That would be my response, anyway.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I will be honest, the first time I heard about the fact that you had interviewed all of these exes, I was horrified by that. I'm such a-- I don't talk to any of my exes, not out of ill will or anything. But it's not a thing I've ever done.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Why don't you keep in touch with them? Is it just done? It's like it's toast and you can't make toast bread?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I feel like the relationship we had exists very much in the time that we were together. And so to revisit it to me feels like going to a past life. I don't know the value of that, I guess, for me, personally.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I would challenge you, I guess. There are so many other ways that it could be, and this sort of dead version is like the least interesting. And what I realized through some of these interviews is if there was love there once, it's kind of always there for me.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Just to say, Evan has been in a happy relationship with his boyfriend for over a decade. But ever since he and Keith broke up 16 years ago, he's wondered, why the card? Why did Keith never want to talk to him again? Why not be friends? Had he missed something when they broke up, done something bad without realizing it? Evan and Keith met in their early 30s. They dated long distance. Evan lived in San Francisco, Keith in Austin.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Evan loved who he was with Keith, said he felt like himself at a higher octave. Keith helped him apply to film school, which he'd always dreamed about. Keith was outgoing, funny. One time when Keith was visiting Evan, Evan came home to find him fake passed out on the living room with a message spelled out in matchsticks. T-T-O-Y-M-M-H. The Thought Of You Makes Me Hot.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: But long distance was hard on them. They broke up a couple of times, would always get back together. They were on one of those breaks when Keith moved to San Francisco, said, look, we could make a real go of this now. Let's make this work. Evan was surprised, taken aback. And instead of jumping in feet first, he said, OK, but let's take our time, not rush things, which Keith did not take well.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: His face changed. Something about his whole body changed. And it did feel like a door closing.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And did that surprise you?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Only because I didn't know that what I said would have that impact.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith broke up with Evan for good. Afterwards, Evan felt like he was walking around in a fog.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: It felt like I was stuck on the wrong timeline. I just felt in a different parallel universe that I wasn't supposed to be in.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Almost immediately, Keith got into a different very serious relationship, which has only further puzzled Evan. They both moved on. Why not become friends now? But Evan's reached out a couple times over the years, and Keith has always been chilly. It's vexed Evan so long, it's become a joke with his friends.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: One of them was in Keith's neighborhood recently and texted Evan about it. His friend joked that he should go take a selfie in front of Keith's house. Evan looked up Keith's address on his computer, copied and pasted it into a text to his friend, hit Send. Then he realized he had accidentally texted Keith's address to Keith.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I screamed when Evan told me this. He thinks he saved it by quickly editing the text to a period, pretending it was an accidental butt text. Did you know can edit texts on an iPhone? I didn't. Recently, he wrote to Keith one last time, asking if he would talk.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I see the email. Keith responded. [GASPS] Oh my god, yes, count me in.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith was game.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: What the fuck? Oh.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: They talk over Zoom, Keith calling in from Brooklyn. I'm with Evan in his apartment in San Francisco, sitting at his dining room table.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Can you hear me?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I can hear you.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Oh my gosh, you sound good.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: You sound good too.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: It takes a minute for them to figure out where to start. The usual awkwardness of a Zoom call is made even worse when it's a man talking to his ex-boyfriend. Evan brings up the last time they talked to see if Keith remembers.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Do you remember the last time that was?

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Was it on, like, Bernal Hill? Or no?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: No, since then. Do you want to guess again? [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: It wasn't on Bernal Hill with my dog?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Oh, yeah, I mean, that happened. I remember that was-- but we've had dinner since then.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: This happens a bunch of times. Whatever Evan brings up, Keith only kind of remembers or doesn't remember at all, like when Evan brings up the time Keith spelled out a secret message in matchsticks, one of his favorite memories of their time together.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: It was "the thought of you makes me hot--" was your new one.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Really? Wow, that's a good one.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith doesn't remember it. What's worse than having someone be angry at you, never want to see you again? I'll tell you what's worse-- finding out they don't think of you at all. Then they get down to business, start talking about the night of their breakup. And Keith explains he'd hoped that at the end of the night, with them finally in the same city, they could really do the thing-- be together. But Evan showed no excitement. In fact, Evan told him, whoa, slow down, one step at a time.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: I think my impression was that you wanted to be together, but you wanted to be friends. I felt like that's what you wanted only.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Only.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: And that was really hard. I didn't want that. I wanted you to feel the same way about me that I did about you. I wanted you to rush over and want to embrace--

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: You wanted the rom-com. You wanted us running to each other in the airport or--

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Yeah, totally.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: That night, Evan actually thought he was saying yes to Keith but just asking to ease into things. Keith had taken it as being friend zoned. They both admit that they didn't do a good job of just saying that to each other. Classic. But as much as Keith remembers that moment, he admits he doesn't really remember what happened after that night.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Did I just ignore you? Please tell me I didn't just ignore you.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: There was a breakup card that you sent in the mail with a hole in it.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: [GASPS] Oh my god. Oh my god. Oh my god. Oh, I remember that. Oh, Lord.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: It's your masterpiece.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Oh my god. Will that be in my retrospective?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: I mean, I'm not proud to admit this, but I probably wanted to hurt you. I'm sorry. That's not a great card to get, particularly one where I put stickers on the outside. Like, that seems like a psychopath.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Like promising one thing and then being another. Like, hey, this is going to be a fun card. I know it's been a little weird between us, but guess what?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Evan and Keith talk for over two hours. At times, their conversation feels a little polite, like two well-therapied gay men talking about their trauma while being recorded by a third well-therapied gay man. But at least Evan has the answer to why Keith had sent the card, which clears the way for Evan to do the thing he came here to do-- make his case that they should have been friends all along.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Yeah. I just feel like I wish that we could have figured out how to be friends, that's all, this whole time.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Do you wish that was possible?

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: I just hadn't really thought about it. As a compartmentalizer-- until you posed that question, I don't think I've really considered it.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Evan just keeps trying to convince him that he's got it all wrong.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I don't-- yeah. I don't understand-- for me, when I connect with someone, when I have the kind of experience I had with you and with other loves of my life, it feels like such a-- like, I'm not doing it-- I'm investing for a reason. And I want someone still in my life. I have wanted you in my life since we broke up.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Mm.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I have needed you.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: [BREATHING DEEPLY]

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: You OK?

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith huffs a couple of times, eventually wiping away some tears. He seems overwhelmed, like he wasn't expecting this depth of feeling from Evan.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: I feel sad. I feel sad about how I handled it, how I communicated, and that I was hurtful to you. And I also am just sad for me and who I was then. So it just is placing me in that small room I paid $300 for or something with no furniture and wanting my life to be something that it wasn't.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: And also, it makes me sad that you-- I think what you said, like, I have needed you as a friend and a person in my life, just makes me feel like just what a waste of time.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Evan is also taking it in, seems flustered.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: It's so weird. It's so weird to be right here right now, Keith. I never thought I'd ever hear any of these things come out of your mouth.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith asks if they can take a break. When we get back on the Zoom, I remind Evan we have one last piece of business-- the accidental text.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: OK. So you can imagine how--

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Evan tells him about how his friend had texted him he was in Keith's neighborhood, their joke about taking a selfie in front of his house.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: So I copied the address, and I texted it to him. And then I realized that I sent it to you.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Really?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Oh, thank god.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Are you serious?

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith gets out his iPhone.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Oh, God, there it is.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: See the period? Now, see where it says edited?

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: You can actually press that and see what--

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Oh! [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Keith taps on the screen, which lets him see the original unedited text with his address.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Oh my god. See, this is the good thing about stalking somebody who doesn't understand their phone.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: The way they're laughing, they sound somewhat like, dare I say, friends? A tension in the room is released. They're more relaxed. And Evan, to my surprise, admits that maybe this all was a bit much.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: There's all these other little details that I have stuck in my head. But I think part of this also is I might just need to let go of some things too. Maybe I don't need to hold on to so many details.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: Yeah. You're a holder on-er.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I'm a holder on-er, for sure. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: About most things in your life, right? Or like--

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: Just you. Just kidding. Just kidding.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: That's good.

segments.speaker: Keith
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: You're a holder on-er-- such an intimate observation. Maybe Evan was right. Maybe digging up all this old stuff with your exes isn't just a masochistic exercise. They say they'll get dinner the next time Keith is in town. The call ends, leaving Evan and me in the apartment.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I'm kind of shocked.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: You are?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Yeah. I really came in today kind of worried for you or not sure what was going to happen. And I feel genuinely convinced that this was a worthwhile exercise, which I'm surprised by. I don't know. I just wanted to say that.

segments.speaker: Evan Roberts
segments.text: I'm so glad you feel that way, actually. I feel vindicated that I convinced you.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I talked to Evan again recently. He said Keith came through town. They didn't get dinner, but he's OK with it. He doesn't have any more questions for him.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tobin Low is a producer in our program. Coming up, a shirt makes judicial history. Did it commit a murder? Did it embezzle funds? Did it violate the Clean Air Act of 1970? Answers in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, "I Want What I Want," stories of people deciding to do things that most of us choose not to do. We have arrived at Act Three of our program. "Act Three, The Lawyer, The Judge, and The Wardrobe." So our show today is about people making unusual choices. And we turn now to a judge making a decision this week that everybody who hears about it seems to agree was a very eccentric decision, not the kind of decision one usually sees.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This happened in a big federal trial in Texas, the Antifa trial of the century, in fact, a kind of landmark case for the Trump administration. One of our producers, Zoe Chace, was there for the first day of the trial on Tuesday. You can't record in this federal courtroom, but Zoe took notes on that first day when they were picking the jury, the part of the process that's called voir dire. In Texas, by the way, everybody calls it "voor dyer." But our Yankee correspondent, Zoe Chace, has no interest in cultural appropriation and is going to stick to her native way of saying it, voir dire. And she now tells us what happened in that courtroom. It was eventful.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So Judge Mark Pittman kind of sweeps into the room. All rise. Here's the judge. He's a Trump appointee from the first Trump administration. He's a bit of a showman, charismatic and kind of exciting to hear from. He has a very strong Texas twang. He welcomes in everybody. And he's like, you should know, I have a pet peeve of people who make fun of jury service. I like to quote Frederick Douglass. He says, we have three boxes that preserve liberty and justice in this country-- the ballot box, the cartridge box, and the jury box. Dramatic pause.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And when they get to the part where you're supposed to start questioning the jurors, the voir dire, he goes first. He leads it. And I'm in the overflow room, so I can't see the jury. But there's 75 or so of them. There's a big group of them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they're going to pick 12 people and I guess a couple of alternates, right?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Right, 12 jurors, three alternates. And the judge starts asking questions to the jurors to see potential bias in the jurors. So he asks them, What kind of experience do you have with law enforcement? which is not an unusual question in a trial like this. And then he goes, do you have strong feelings about what ICE has been doing? Are you pro or con?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And let me just say, he's asking about ICE because this particular case has-- is it nine defendants, Zoe?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yeah, at this point.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they were protesting ICE's actions. They were at an ICE facility.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Right. I mean, the government would say that they went to attack an ICE facility. And in fact, one of the defendants did shoot a local police officer, and that officer was wounded. And the government's arguing that these defendants were organized, they're part of an Antifa cell. This is the government's big case, where they're hoping to show that there is an Antifa. It's a domestic terror group. And you can win big convictions on that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And we should say, the defense says none of this is true. They say they were not a group. They say these people were not planning an attack. They say they were protesters protesting ICE.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Right. And so the judge is asking these potential jurors, what are your feelings about ICE? And the way he asked, it's like, do any of you have strong feelings about what ICE is doing? Pro or con is what he says. And he sort of has people raise their hands. But juror after juror is raising their hand, and they're saying, yes, I am very upset about what ICE is doing. I do not like what ICE is doing.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So this is Tarrant County, Texas. It's like a purple district in the middle of the country. And this is like the definition of a random sample of people. But at least according to people around me, like local reporters and people who live in the area, this doesn't sound like Tarrant County, Texas to them, just person after person saying they're upset about ICE.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And I don't know. The judge did bring up Minneapolis. And since Minneapolis, a majority of Americans don't approve of what ICE is doing. So maybe that's what this is an example of.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, wait. And did anybody, when they raised their hand, did they say, yes, I have a strong feeling about ICE, that President Trump is finally delivering on his promises, and I'm very much in favor of what ICE is doing? Does anybody say that?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: No. It's just person after person, no ICE, boo, ICE. And the judge was very focused on this follow-up, which was, OK, can you put aside your feelings about ICE? However strong they are, can you leave them outside the courtroom?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which does not seem like a bad question.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Not at all. But a lot of times, they would be like, I don't know if I can. I will try, but I am really upset. And the judge-- which seems honest. The judge would kind of push them. So does that mean you can't follow my instructions under the Constitution to consider only what's in front of you? And then they would eventually be like, yes, I can follow your instructions. Most of them ended up saying yes after some pushing from him.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And he kept using as an example-- he kept being like, I'm an Aggie, so you know how I feel about the University of Texas. But if the University of Texas was on trial, I could put my feelings aside and judge the University of Texas fairly. If I can do that, can you do that? And finally, one of the potential jurors in the back and forth said, "Sir, respectfully, a college rivalry is not the same as human rights."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And this anti-ICE stuff comes up again. Then when the prosecution gets a chance to ask their questions, one woman just starts out saying, "I don't think I can be on this jury. I have two family members who have died after being deported." Another one is like, "ICE's tactics, the conditions in the detention facilities are horrific. I don't know if I could put my feelings aside." And the government attorney is like, "I'm sorry, could you repeat that?" She's like, "Horrific!"

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So things are not going so great for the prosecutors. What happens when the defense attorneys get up and get to ask their questions of the potential jurors?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yeah. The defense comes up, and right away, things go awry. The story really changes here. The first defense attorney comes to ask her questions. This is defense attorney Marquita Clayton. And she brings sort of a poster board to help with her questioning. And the judge sees this and he, like, freaks. He's like, what is that? Has the prosecution seen that? I haven't seen that. You are not allowed to bring props in here-- maybe in state court. This is federal court. He's very upset, and the poster board is hastily put away.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And then she's asking some questions about whether or not you can bring a gun to a protest, what the potential jurors think about that. It's a bit of a confusingly phrased question, to be honest. And it's taking a while because she's going juror by juror. And the judge interrupts. He's impatient. He just goes, defense counsel, is this really how you want to use your time? Something like, I've been the most generous federal judge in the history of the world, given you guys 90 minutes. This has been going on for 22 minutes. I really think you should consider whether this is a good use of your time-- something to that effect.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And I want to note, this attorney he's rebuking is a Black woman. She's the only Black woman attorney, as far as I can see, in a room full of attorneys. The judge-- white guy. So that's the scene. And then he goes, in fact, you all better have a little visit and think about whether this is how you really want to proceed-- or something to that effect. He's just--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You mean you-- defense attorneys, get together, have a timeout--

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: --talk about whether this is what you want to do?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Because I'm here to tell you it's not. And so there's this little recess. And then when he comes back, he's hot. He's upset. And he just starts right into what he's upset about. And he's like, there are very clear rules in this court about having demonstratives in the courtroom.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Demonstrative is the poster board.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Right, bringing any prop with you to the courtroom-- and also about what you're wearing in the courtroom. And this attorney, I have just realized, is wearing a shirt.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This attorney means the defense attorney.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yeah. And indeed, this attorney is wearing a shirt-- she's wearing a blazer over it-- that I happened to see earlier in the bathroom. So I saw it up close. It's kind of checkered. It's these little squares, smaller than a cigarette packet, of civil rights leaders. Martin Luther King is on there. And it's kind of iconic images of the civil rights movement. And when I saw it, I was like, oh, she put that on because Jesse Jackson just died. We just got the news he died that morning.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: So it's a shirt honoring protesters. And the judge is like, we've been talking about peaceful protest for 20 minutes, and you're wearing a shirt with peaceful protesters on it. And the jurors can't unsee that. You can't use your clothing to influence the jury. He says, that shirt has a politically charged message. It's as if the prosecutor were wearing ICE-friendly pins or a shirt with Donald Trump on it, riding an eagle, flying an ICE flag. I'm sure the defense would go ballistic if that happened. This is why in England, they wear black robes and wigs.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I don't think this can be corrected by any type of instruction to the jury. And so I have no choice but to declare a mistrial. Everyone is like, what? Because this is a crazy turn of events. That's like a nuclear bomb, to just drop the entire trial and start it over because of this woman's shirt.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, and what do people do?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Well, everyone's just surprised. Everybody is stunned in the room. And the judge is kind of like, I'm going to see what all the attorneys think about this. I should say also that the jury is not back from the break. The potential jury is not seeing this whole back and forth. Anyway, the judge pulls all the attorneys, like, do you guys think there should be a mistrial? And even the government, whose case was supposedly hurt beyond repair because of this shirt, they seem taken aback. They seem surprised by this turn of events. And they say, basically, I don't know. They don't cosine the mistrial.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They don't ask for a mistrial.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: They don't ask for a mistrial. And OK, it is against the rules of the courtroom to wear a shirt like this, a shirt with a message on it. I talked to a federal prosecutor from the same district who agreed with the judge that it could undermine the whole trial. She said, if you're going to throw out the whole case and restart it because of a shirt, this was just the first day. You're not losing much.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Someone else I talked to, a federal defense attorney in Texas, said she'd never wear a shirt like that to court. But she also said, I don't agree with the judge that there was no other option besides a mistrial. There are lots of options. You can sanction the lawyer. You could fine them. You can tell the jury to disregard what they've seen. You can ask the jury if they even saw it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So mistrials are rare.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Mistrials are extremely rare. The judge himself said he'd never called one before in his whole career. Then the judge-- it's not over. He says he needs a break to go review the law, and he kind of sweeps out of there. I go back into the hallway, and I see one of the defense attorneys. And I'm like, "Dude, what is going on? Like, is there going to be a mistrial because of her shirt?" And he's like, "It's not the shirt. The judge doesn't like the jury panel." And I'm like, "Why?" And he's like, "Because they hate ICE." And that the shirt, the shirt is the MacGuffin in order to restart this whole thing and get a new jury pool to choose from.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And do you think that might be true?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I mean, that is pure speculation. That is not what the judge said. That's not the stated reason for calling a mistrial. And later, that defense lawyer pulled it back. He was like, I really don't know. But it was a significant thing, how many people were against ICE over and over, and people saying they wouldn't be able to put their feelings aside over and over.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How many people was it?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: It was 18 to 20. I know we're talking about a jury pool of 70-plus people. But the way the process works, the prosecution would not necessarily be able to block all the jurors who hated ICE, if that's what they wanted to do, just because of the rules of the game.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But if the judge, in fact, is doing this because he doesn't want people who have strong feelings against these law enforcement figures to be on a jury that's about these law enforcement figures, that's not so strange. It seems like that would happen in any courtroom for any trial involving law enforcement figures.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: Yeah. That's not a weird goal at all. It's potential bias, their feelings about ICE. It's not strange the judge would want that at all. But it is strange to call a mistrial. And there is a clue that something else was going on with this judge, which was at the end of this strange day in court, he calls the jury back in, and he gives this little speech. And it kind of comes out of nowhere. He talks again about how much jury service matters, and this should be a place where you can set your personal politics aside.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: And then he says, I'm disgusted by where America is today, how hopelessly divided we are over politics. In the 1850s, Abraham Lincoln said, "A house divided against itself cannot stand." I don't want my sons to fight in the next civil war. We have to find a way to turn down the anger and the hatred.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, what?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: I know. Everyone around me was looking at each other like, what was that? And I think he was frustrated by how impossible it seemed to create a room right now that is what a courtroom is supposed to be-- neutral ground. He said over and over during the whole day how important it is to get an unbiased jury that only considers the facts in front of them, to have a room with no politics in it. The shirt violated that, and possibly the jurors' answers about ICE.

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: But of course, the problem in trying to create an apolitical trial is the very premise of this trial is so political. It's about this stuff being debated literally every day, all the time. It's ICE, Trump, Antifa, Antifa versus ICE. Maybe there's a room somewhere you could discuss it objectively. I just don't know if that room exists in the United States.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK. And so, Zoe, I think what you're saying is, I think your big conclusion today is-- you're saying we are a very divided country?

segments.speaker: Zoe Chace
segments.text: You heard it here first.
